newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's future leader to Beijing for talks.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's future leader to Beijing for talks.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader, in the midst of assembling his post-colonial administration, prepared on Friday to fly to Beijing on a weekend visit for his first set of working level talks.
Jockeying for position is rife in the British colony as British influence wanes in the countdown to the mid-1997 handover to China, a date just 179 days away.

Pro-Beijing groups and individuals are vying for places in the administration being formed by Tung Chee-hwa, a 59-year-old shipping magnate selected by a Beijing-appointed panel on December 11 as Hong Kong's Chief Executive-designate.

Tung has yet to name his team to take over from the colonial administration headed by British governor Chris Patten and his every meeting is carefully watched by Hong Kong people eager to divine the identities of their future leaders.
Tung said his one-day visit to Beijing on Saturday would focus on government funding and the legal status of a Provisional Legislature, which China will install when it takes over on July 1.

The trip is Tung's second to the Chinese capital since his appointment and, in contrast to the largely ceremonial occasion in mid-December when he was congratulated by Chinese Premier Li Peng, is likely to be a lower-key and more business-like affair.

"This visit will be very different from the last time when leaders of the central government received me," the former shipping magnate told reporters on Thursday. "This time I am just going for work."

Tung said he would discuss the constitutional status of the Provisional Legislature, which faces a legal challenge from Hong Kong's largest pro-democracy party, which argues it is illegal for two rival legislatures to operate simulataneously.

The Democratic Party fared the best in the 1995 elections but its deputies will lose their seats in the elected legislative council when Beijing dissolves the chamber, undoing at a stroke electoral reforms introduced by the British.

The threats of a court challenge from Democratic Party leaders mean the Provisional Legislature, selected last month by the same 400-strong Beijing-vetted panel responsible for Tung's appointment, is expected to meet in China and not Hong Kong.
Tung did not say whether he would ask the Chinese parliament to pass a law to endorse the Provisional Legislature in order to shield it against a legal challenge,

But he did said he would continue to try and coax the Democrats to accept it as reality during a meeting with them next Thursday. "The Provisional Legislature has the right to exist. I hope that everyone... can accept it," he said.
While Tung faces difficulties in wooing the democratic lobby, he faces no shortage of supplicants from many sectors of Hong Kong society keen to join the team.

Pro-Beijing politicians, unions and business groups with strong mainland links have queued up enthusiastically in recent weeks to express their support for Tung and advertise their qualifications for positions of high office.
Within days of his appointment, Tung publicly invited Hong Kong's popular chief civil servant Anson Chan to stay on in her post as the number two official in the Hong Kong administration.
Chan accepted his invitation in a move which won acclaim in Hong Kong.
Tung, despite a heavy schedule of meetings with Hong Kong's elite, has since refused even to hint at who else might be in the running.
